title: A disabled theatre troupe makes able-bodied people the discriminated minority — and it is not asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This is not a lament — it is a wish-fulfilment story written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; its value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgement can skip it.
who: People in charity work, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why integration cannot rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission call-out at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is a widespread phenomenon
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at festivals, her feeling was that it was "like walking a little dog or cat". Later she got her first computer, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. After getting the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another mother, who is visually impaired, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterwards she fought her husband's family for custody. These testimonies made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house is not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs, hanging things all over the chairs and hauling load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she did not call on able-bodied friends who can walk upright, who could have finished the move in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she did not know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even have the chance to meet, "you have no chance of integration at all". This was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
points.body: Leyi Theatre's first play, Ni Zhuan Wei Lai (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people into disabled people, who through electronic eyes, cochlear implants and similar technology become new humans; the remaining few able-bodied people, because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war", become original sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic is that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights able-bodied people have to fight for — she calls this writing a wish-fulfilment story for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to spare his son from suffering because of his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with killing his father, and the courtroom scenes open up discussion of original sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning to be his partner at an audition; his first reaction was bewilderment: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says there is already an international form of blind and deaf performers sharing a stage, with the deaf person's hand on the visually impaired person's hand so the latter can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says he had grown up around deaf people, but at the time he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, for whom "communication was absolutely impossible", a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors wear earphones and cheat on stage
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them on stage seamlessly, so the director could not assess them at all and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director does not know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing on the side, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

points.h: She received the best production award in the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Ni Zhuan Wei Lai was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us". In the end they won the Best Production award, the highest prize of the Nanjing New Theatre Festival, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. At the same moment the news reached the ICU, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was specially invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first integrated disability production and the only piece in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
points.body: The second play, Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a foetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health condition and family environment, and the foetus itself decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child that you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, and a family that favours boys over girls; the last story is adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors could not get through the script because their life experiences were so eerily similar, differing only in the type of condition. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had the chance to do it again, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao, however, changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice at all.

points.h: The same question, and Cai Cong gives the opposite answer
points.body: The episode sets the deaf couple in Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng against the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?

A congenital condition in which the internal organs are completely reversed from the normal position; Yaoyao has this condition.

This play makes you think; the sincerity of the performance covers the flaws in technique. What is most striking is the troupe's refusal to be pitied.
